en: The *Buddhabhāṣitānūpavāta-sūtra*, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavat was staying in the city of Vajji, named Anūpavāta.
At that time, the Blessed One rose from his afternoon rest and addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Come, Ānanda!"
"Let us go together to the waters of Lake Āyāgapata; let us bathe together.
"So be it, World-Honored One! Thus did the Venerable Ānanda receive the instruction of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, together with the Venerable Ānanda and his retinue of bhikṣus, went to the waters of the Āyudhavatī Pond.

Having arrived, he stood on the bank of the Āyudhavatī Pond, removed his robes and placed them on the bank, bathed in the waters of the Āyudhavatī Pond, and having emerged from the water, stood on the bank and wiped away the moisture.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda!
The negligent Devadatta has lost his standing and shall fall into an evil destiny; he will dwell in hell for an eon, and it will be difficult to save him.”
"Ānanda! Have you not heard these words from a certain bhikṣu? [He replied:
"I have been told that Devadatta shall fall into an evil destiny, remaining in hell for one kalpa, and will be difficult to save."
For what reason?
Indeed, World-Honored One!
Have you not heard this?
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
I heard these words from a certain bhikṣu.
"How was this, worthy Ānanda?"
Does the Blessed One know the thoughts in Devadatta’s mind and his wicked and false conduct through some other means?
Or does the Blessed One now declare categorically that this Devadatta shall fall into the evil destinies and dwell in hell for one kalpa, from which he will be difficult to save?
Ānanda, among these monks—
whether they be seniors, juniors, or junior monks of little wisdom— whoever has doubts regarding what the Tathāgata has spoken.
Why is this? Ānanda!

Among the devas, the world, Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all gods and humans, I do not see anyone whom I have predicted would fall into an evil destiny and remain in hell for an eon, being difficult to save, such as Devadatta.
Why is this? Ānanda!
I have declared categorically that Devadatta will fall into an evil destiny, remaining in hell for an eon, and will be difficult to save.
"Ānanda, I do not see even a hair’s breadth of white dharma in Devadatta; had I seen any,
I would not have declared categorically that Devadatta will fall into an evil destination, dwell in hell for an eon, and be difficult to save."
Therefore, Ānanda!

I do not see even a hair’s breadth of white dharma in Devadatta; for this reason, I have declared categorically that Devadatta will fall into the evil destinies and dwell in hell for an eon, from which he will be difficult to rescue.
It is just as if, Ānanda,
not far from a city or village there were a large latrine filled with excrement, and a certain person fell into it, sinking so deep that his body was no longer visible.
Suppose there were someone who, out of compassion for him, wishing to benefit and rescue him, and desiring to bring him peace and security, walked about that great latrine looking for him, thinking:
"Is there perhaps even a spot as small as a hair on this man that is not soiled? I shall take hold of him and pull him out."
He moved about within that great latrine, inspecting it, and there was not a single spot, even as small as a hair, that was not defiled, yet he caused that person to be rescued and delivered.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
I do not see even a single white dharma in Devadatta, as small as a hair;
if there were such a thing, I would not have declared categorically that Devadatta will fall into the evil destinies and remain in hell for an eon, from which he is difficult to rescue.
Therefore, Ānanda!

I do not see even a single hair’s breadth of white dharma in Devadatta; for this reason, I have declared categorically that Devadatta will fall into an evil destiny, remaining in hell for an eon, and will be difficult to save.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda shed tears from his eyes; with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One, saying:
“How extraordinary, O Blessed One! How marvelous!”
"Now, the World-Honored One has declared categorically that this Devadatta will fall into an evil destination, remaining in hell for an eon, and will be difficult to save. "It is so, Ānanda!"
Thus it is, Ānanda!
I have declared with certainty that this Devadatta shall fall into an evil destiny, remaining in hell for an eon, difficult to rescue.
"You, Ānanda!
You should listen from the Tathāgata as he analyzes the marks of the faculties of a Great Man; you shall increase your faith and devotion toward the Tathāgata, and joy will arise in your mind."
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Now is the time, Blessed One!
This is the time for a skillful resolution. We pray only that the Blessed One [would speak]!"
"I shall explain to the bhikṣus the distinguishing marks of the faculties of a Great Man.
Having heard this from the Blessed One, these bhikṣus will surely [act accordingly].
“Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
"Listen, and attend well to it; I shall speak for you.
"So be it, World-Honored One!"
The Venerable Ānanda received the instruction of the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said to him:
“In this regard, Ānanda!”

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts in the mind of a person: whether this person is associated with wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows the course of that person’s mental activity: "In this person, wholesome dharmas have ceased and unwholesome dharmas have arisen; in this person, wholesome dharmas have ceased and unwholesome dharmas have been acquired. Although their existing roots of goodness have not been severed, they shall yet further attain goodness upon this basis of goodness."
In this way, for such a person, the dharma of the purification of the mind becomes supreme;
it is just as, Ānanda, when the sun is about to rise, all darkness is completely extinguished and great light is attained.
What do you think, Ānanda?
Once the sun has risen and it is time for the meal, does any darkness remain that is not dispelled? Is there anything that is not illuminated?
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One! It is so, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata knows the mental inclinations and conduct of a person—whether that person is associated with wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows their mental inclinations and conduct: ‘In this person, wholesome dharmas have ceased and unwholesome dharmas have arisen; wholesome dharmas have ceased and unwholesome dharmas have been acquired. Yet, since their existing roots of goodness have not been severed, they shall further attain wholesome dharmas. In this way, this person reaches the state of pure mental clarity.”
It is just as if, Ānanda,
there were a seed that was neither damaged nor broken, neither rotten nor cut, not injured by the wind, and kept safely within a vessel.
Suppose that farmer, having thoroughly leveled his field and plowed it, sows seed therein, and the heavens provide timely rain and moisture.
What do you think, Ānanda?
“Would you be able to obtain many seeds?
“Certainly, World-Honored One!
“In this way, Ānanda!”

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of a single person: whether this person is associated with wholesome qualities or unwholesome qualities. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows their thoughts and conduct; he knows that for this person, wholesome qualities have ceased and unwholesome qualities have arisen, and that while wholesome qualities have ceased, unwholesome qualities have been acquired. Yet, because their existing roots of goodness have not been severed, they will further attain goodness upon that goodness; thus, this person reaches the state of pure mental clarity.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
In this way, the Tathāgata speaks of the marks of the faculties of a great man; likewise, he fully understands all that the dharmas of the Tathāgata lead toward.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of a person: whether this person is associated with wholesome qualities or unwholesome qualities. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows their thoughts and conduct: that for this person, wholesome qualities have ceased and unwholesome qualities have arisen; that for this person, wholesome qualities have ceased and they have acquired unwholesome qualities; and that although they possess roots of goodness which have not yet been severed, all shall eventually be severed—thus, for this person, there is the quality of severance.
It is just as, Ānanda,
when at the hour of late afternoon the sun is about to set, all light is extinguished and it becomes dark.
What do you think, Ānanda?
"When that sun sets, is it not the case that the light ceases entirely and becomes darkness?
"Indeed it is, World-Honored One. "So it is, Ānanda!"

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of a person: whether that person is associated with wholesome qualities or unwholesome qualities. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows their thoughts and conduct: "In this person, wholesome qualities have ceased and unwholesome qualities have arisen; in this person, wholesome qualities have ceased and unwholesome qualities have been acquired. Although there were previously roots of goodness that were not severed, all of them shall now be severed. Thus, Ānanda, this person possesses qualities that will be severed, just as follows: [The Buddha continued: "Suppose, Ānanda, there is a great reservoir of water. A man comes along carrying a small amount of water in a bowl. He thinks: 'I shall pour this water into the great reservoir. He pours it in, and it is lost within the great reservoir. He thinks again: 'I shall pour more water into the great reservoir,' and he pours it in, and it is lost within the great reservoir. Even though he has poured in a little water, it is lost within the great reservoir. In the same way, Ānanda, when a person’s wholesome qualities are severed, they are like that small amount of water poured into the great reservoir."

Suppose there were a seed—unbroken, unimpaired, undecayed, uncut, and not damaged by wind—which had been placed securely in a vessel. After a farmer had thoroughly leveled and plowed his field, he sowed that seed therein. If the heavens did not send down rain in due season, what do you think, Ānanda?
"Would one obtain many seeds?
"No, World-Honored One."

“In this way, Ānanda, the Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of a person’s mind: ‘This person is possessed of wholesome qualities. Later, the Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of that person’s mind: ‘The wholesome qualities of this person have ceased and unwholesome qualities have arisen; this person has lost their wholesome qualities and acquired unwholesome ones. Those roots of goodness that were not yet severed shall all be severed. Thus, this person possesses the quality of severance.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!
When the Tathāgata has thus taught the characteristics of the faculties of a great person, he has already known with certainty that such dharmas arise from such dharmas.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of a certain person; I do not see in that person even a hair’s breadth of white dharma. This person is consistently filled with evil and unwholesome dharmas, bound by fetters, and will receive the retribution of suffering and heat, undergoing birth, old age, sickness, and death. Thus, when this person’s body perishes at death, they are reborn in hell.
It is just as if, Ānanda, there were seeds that were broken, split, or cut;

they had been damaged by the wind and were placed in a vessel in an unstable manner. A householder farmer did not plow the field deeply nor level the ground well, yet he sowed the seeds. If the heavens then sent rain at the proper time, what do you think, Ānanda?
“Would there not be many? “No, World-Honored One.”
“In this way, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of a person’s mind; I do not see in this person even a hair’s breadth of wholesome dharma. This person is single-mindedly filled with evil and unwholesome dharmas, bound by fetters, and will receive the retribution of suffering and heat, undergoing birth, old age, sickness, and death. Thus, when this person’s body perishes, they will be reborn in hell.”
"In this way, Ānanda!
Thus does the Tathāgata speak of the marks of the faculties of a Great Man; in this way, the Tathāgata fully understands the mutual arising of all phenomena.
Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda joined his palms toward the World-Honored One and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!
Beyond these three types of persons already mentioned, can there be further three types of persons who cannot be described as either attainable or unattainable?"
“Ānanda! the Blessed One said. “This, Ānanda!”

The Tathāgata may know the thoughts and conduct of a person: that this person is associated with unwholesome dharmas or associated with wholesome dharmas. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows their thoughts and conduct: that unwholesome dharmas have ceased and wholesome dharmas have arisen in this person; that unwholesome dharmas have ceased and they have attained wholesome dharmas; and that although there are still unwholesome roots which have not been severed, they shall further attain wholesome dharmas through these wholesome dharmas, such that for this person, those [unwholesome] dharmas will eventually come to cessation.
"It is just as if, Ānanda, there were a fire burning, blazing, and spontaneously flaming, and someone were to throw dry grass and wood into it. What do you think, Ānanda?"
“Would there be much fire?
“Indeed, World-Honored One! “So it is, Ānanda!”

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and conduct of a person: whether this person is associated with unwholesome qualities or associated with wholesome qualities. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows that person’s thoughts and conduct: "In this person, unwholesome qualities have ceased and wholesome qualities have arisen; unwholesome qualities have been extinguished and wholesome qualities have been attained. Although there remains an unwholesome root that has not been severed, through which further unwholesome qualities will arise, such that these qualities of this person are destined to perish."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
When the Tathāgata speaks of the marks of the faculties of a great person, the Tathāgata knows the arising of phenomena from phenomena in this way, and he understands them all with certainty.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and actions of a person: whether this person is associated with unwholesome states or wholesome states. At a later time, the Tathāgata knows that person’s thoughts and actions; he sees that for this person, unwholesome states have ceased and wholesome states have arisen, and that while unwholesome states have ceased, wholesome states have been attained. Although unwholesome roots previously existed and were not yet severed, they shall all now be severed. Thus, this person will ultimately attain the state of complete purity.

It is just as if, Ānanda, there were a fire burning, blazing, and spontaneously flaming; and suppose someone were to take that fire and place it on dry ground or upon a stone—what do you think, Ānanda?
“Would that fire burn more?
“No, indeed, World-Honored One.”

“Thus it is, Ānanda! The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and the conduct of a person’s mind: that this person is associated with unwholesome dharmas or associated with wholesome dharmas. Later, the Tathāgata knows the thoughts and the conduct of that person’s mind: that for this person, unwholesome dharmas have ceased and wholesome dharmas have arisen; that for this person, unwholesome dharmas have ceased and they have attained wholesome dharmas; and that although unwholesome roots previously existed and were not yet severed, they shall all now be severed. In this way, this person will ultimately reach the state of pure dharma.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!
In this way the Tathāgata teaches the characteristics of the faculties of a Great Man; in this way the Tathāgata’s dharmas arise from one another, and he fully understands them all.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and the conduct of a person; I do not see even a hair’s breadth of unwholesome conduct in this person. This person is consistently filled with wholesome qualities, wholesome conduct, and wholesome results; his body is in accord with a favorable state of existence, and thus this person shall attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.
It is just as if, Ānanda, there were a fire that had been extinguished, becoming cool and free from heat, and someone were to place dry grass and wood into it. What do you think, Ānanda?
"Could one obtain fire? "No,
World-Honored One."
"Thus it is, Ānanda!

The Tathāgata knows the thoughts and the conduct of a certain person; I do not see even a hair’s breadth of unwholesome conduct in this person. This person is single-mindedly devoted to the practice of wholesome dharmas and their wholesome fruits; such a person is destined for parinirvāṇa in this very life."
Thus it is, Ānanda!
The Tathāgata has taught the characteristics of the faculties of a great person; in this way, the Tathāgata fully understands the mutual arising of all phenomena (dharmas). This, Ānanda!

That is to say, among these first three types of persons: one person possesses the dharma of purity; two types of persons possess the dharma of cessation; and three types of persons, upon the dissolution of the body, fall into the evil destinies and the hells.

That is to say, regarding these latter three types of persons: one person possesses the nature of cessation; two types of persons possess the nature of purification; and three types of persons, having seen the Dharma, shall attain parinirvāṇa.
"Ānanda, this has been taught by me as the mark of the faculties of a Great Man; as the World-Honored One should act with compassion and for the benefit of his disciples, so have I taught it to you."
"Now you should sit in a quiet place or at the foot of a tree and practice meditative reflection; do not be negligent, lest you later feel regret.
This is what I have said; this is my instruction."
Thus spoke the Buddha.
Having heard what the World-Honored One had said, those bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
This concludes the *Anūha-vāta-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
